Adult female Drouhard's shrew tenrecs (Microgale drouhardi) attain a maximum body mass of 14 grams [Wwi = 14 grams], a figure that represents the upper end of the reported range for this species. This adult mass is notably modest, and the physical development of a neonate begins from a surprisingly small starting point. Newborn individuals weigh approximately 1.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.8 grams], a birth mass that reflects the relatively altricial condition of the neonate. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the gestation period for this species is completed in 61 days [tg = 61 days]. This duration of gestation is consistent with the extended embryonic development observed in other tenrecids of similar size, likely reflecting the energetic constraints of early organogenesis in a small-bodied eutherian mammal. The progression from zygote formation to parturition thus represents a considerable physiological investment for a female whose own adult mass does not exceed 14 grams [Wwi = 14 grams].

Following parturition, the neonatal individuals depend entirely on maternal milk during an initial period of development. The suckling juvenile stage is relatively abbreviated in this species, with weaning occurring at 29 days after birth [tx = 29 days after birth] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This key developmental milestone, marking the end of maternal provisioning and the nutritional independence onset of the offspring, takes place at the standard thermal reference of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. The transition to solid food at this age allows the young to begin exploiting the invertebrate prey that constitutes their primary diet. After weaning, the juvenile enters a protracted sub-adult phase characterized by slow somatic growth. Sexual maturation is not achieved quickly; puberty, defined here as the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation, is reached at 639 days after birth [tp = 639 days after birth] under the same controlled thermal conditions at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This delay of nearly two years before reproductive maturity is a striking feature of the species' life history.

The longevity of Microgale drouhardi is considerable for a mammal of its diminutive stature. Under captive conditions maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan extends to approximately 2,117 days [am = approximately 2,117 days], a duration that translates to roughly 5.8 years. This extended lifespan is notably greater than what is typically documented for eutherians of a comparable body mass, which often exhibit faster life-history paces and shorter maximum longevities. The geriatric death of the oldest documented individuals in a laboratory setting occurred well past the age at first reproduction, with some females continuing to show signs of reproductive activity even into their fifth year. Such a pattern of slow aging and extended post-reproductive survival aligns with the broader life-history strategy of the Tenrecidae, a family that is known for its variable metabolic rates and relatively low basal energetic demands compared to other insectivorous mammals.

The maximum reproductive rate for this species has been inferred from data on the closely related congener Microgale talazaci. Under the same ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], each litter typically contains 2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 pups per litter], and females are capable of producing 3 litters annually [F_R_i = 3 litters annually]. This combination of a modest litter size and a relatively high annual frequency of reproductive events suggests that females invest a substantial portion of their annual energy budget into offspring production. This reproductive pattern is adaptive in the unpredictable montane forest environment of Madagascar, where seasonal fluctuations in invertebrate prey abundance can be severe.

Basal metabolic rate measurements provide further insight into the energetic physiology of Microgale drouhardi. Respirometry trials conducted at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] have recorded a resting oxygen consumption of 28.39 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 28.39 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is consistent with the reduced metabolic rates that characterize many tenrecid species, which can enter daily torpor to conserve energy during periods of low resource availability. The observed basal oxygen consumption of 28.39 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 28.39 milliliters of oxygen per hour] is relatively low for a mammal of 14 grams, a finding that supports the hypothesis that Microgale drouhardi employs a conservative energetic strategy at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This low maintenance requirement may help explain the species' ability to sustain its protracted developmental schedule and extended lifespan in a resource-limited environment.
